hints: Focus on what the mass spectrometer sees for an $\text{O}_2^+$ ion, it is the total mass of the two oxygen atoms joined together.
List every possible pair you can make from $^{16}\text{O}$, $^{17}\text{O}$ and $^{18}\text{O}$, starting with $^{16}\text{O}$ paired with each isotope.
Check your list for different pairs that add up to the same total mass, since those give only one peak, then count the unique masses left.
walkthrough:
**What makes a peak for O2+**

Think side by side with me. A peak appears at each different $m/z$ value. For $\text{O}_2^+$ the charge is +1, so $m/z$ is simply the sum of the two oxygen mass numbers.

$$m/z = \text{mass of first O atom} + \text{mass of second O atom}$$

**List all possible pairs**

Let us be systematic and pair each isotope with itself and the others. This gives six combinations in total.

$$^{16}\text{O}^{16}\text{O} = 32, \quad ^{16}\text{O}^{17}\text{O} = 33, \quad ^{16}\text{O}^{18}\text{O} = 34$$
$$^{17}\text{O}^{17}\text{O} = 34, \quad ^{17}\text{O}^{18}\text{O} = 35, \quad ^{18}\text{O}^{18}\text{O} = 36$$

**Spot the duplicate mass**

Here is the clever part. Two different pairs give the same total. Both $^{16}\text{O}^{18}\text{O}$ and $^{17}\text{O}^{17}\text{O}$ add to 34, so they appear as one peak, not two.

$$16 + 18 = 34 = 17 + 17$$

**Count unique peaks**

So the distinct $m/z$ values are only 32, 33, 34, 35 and 36. That is five separate peaks for $\text{O}_2^+.$

options.A: 3 counts only the three isotopes $^{16}\text{O}$, $^{17}\text{O}$ and $^{18}\text{O}$. This forgets that the ion is $\text{O}_2^+$, which contains two atoms, so many combined masses are possible.
options.B: 5 is correct. The six pair combinations give masses 32, 33, 34, 34, 35, 36, but 34 occurs twice ($^{16}\text{O}^{18}\text{O}$ and $^{17}\text{O}^{17}\text{O}$), leaving 5 unique $m/z$ values: 32, 33, 34, 35, 36.
options.C: 6 counts every ordered pairing as different: 16-16, 16-17, 16-18, 17-17, 17-18, 18-18. It misses that $^{16}\text{O}^{18}\text{O}$ and $^{17}\text{O}^{17}\text{O}$ have the same mass (34) and so give one shared peak.
options.D: 9 comes from calculating $3 \times 3 = 9$ and treating $^{16}\text{O}^{17}\text{O}$ as different from $^{17}\text{O}^{16}\text{O}$. In mass spectrometry order does not matter, only total mass, and duplicate masses also merge.
